topics.name: Personal Pronouns
topics.description: German personal pronouns: ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie

knowledge_points.explanation: 'ich' (I) is always lowercase unless it starts a sentence.
'du' is used for friends, family, and children.
'er' replaces masculine nouns.
'sie' (lowercase) means 'she' when the verb is conjugated for 3rd person singular.
'es' replaces neuter nouns and is used in impersonal expressions like weather.
'wir' (we) always takes the same verb form as the infinitive.
'ihr' is used to address multiple people informally.
'sie' (lowercase) means 'they'; 'Sie' (capitalized) is the formal 'you' for polite address.

topics.name: Verb "sein" (to be)
topics.description: Conjugation of the irregular verb 'sein' for all personal pronouns

knowledge_points.explanation: 'sein' is highly irregular. For 'ich': sein → bin.
For 'du': sein → bist.
For 'er/sie/es': sein → ist.
For 'wir': sein → sind.
For 'ihr': sein → seid.
For 'sie' (they) and 'Sie' (formal you): sein → sind.

prompt_data.rule: Negate 'sein' by placing 'nicht' after the conjugated form

knowledge_points.explanation: To negate 'sein', place 'nicht' after the conjugated verb: 'Er ist nicht hier.'

prompt_data.rule: For yes/no questions with 'sein', put the verb first

knowledge_points.explanation: In yes/no questions, the verb comes first: 'Bist du Student?'

topics.name: Verb "haben" (to have)
topics.description: Conjugation of the irregular verb 'haben' for all personal pronouns

knowledge_points.explanation: For 'ich': haben → habe (regular pattern).
For 'du': haben → hast (the 'b' drops out).
For 'er/sie/es': haben → hat (the 'b' drops out).
For 'wir': haben → haben (same as infinitive).
For 'ihr': haben → habt.
For 'sie' (they) and 'Sie' (formal): haben → haben (same as infinitive).

prompt_data.rule: Use 'kein/keine/keinen' instead of 'nicht ein' to negate nouns with 'haben'

knowledge_points.explanation: With 'haben' + noun, negate with 'kein' (not 'nicht ein'): 'Ich habe kein Auto.'

prompt_data.english: I am hungry (lit: I have hunger)

knowledge_points.explanation: German uses 'haben' for states like hunger/thirst: 'Hunger haben' = to be hungry.

topics.name: Nominative Articles
topics.description: Definite (der, die, das) and indefinite (ein, eine) articles in nominative case with example nouns

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der' is the definite article for masculine nouns in the nominative case.
'der Stuhl' is masculine. The plural adds an umlaut: Stühle.
'der Mann' is masculine. Plural: die Männer (with umlaut and -er).
'die' is the definite article for feminine nouns. 'die Frau' can also mean 'Mrs.' or 'wife'.
'die' is the definite article for feminine nouns. Many nouns ending in '-e' are feminine.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Die Katze schläft auf dem Sofa.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'die Katze' is feminine. Nouns ending in '-e' are often feminine.
'das' is the definite article for neuter nouns.
'das Kind' is neuter. Diminutives (-chen, -lein) are always neuter in German.
'das Haus' is neuter. Plural: die Häuser (with umlaut and -er).
'ein' is the indefinite article for masculine and neuter nouns in nominative.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Eine Frau wartet an der Haltestelle.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'eine' is the indefinite article for feminine nouns in nominative.
'ein' is used for both masculine and neuter nouns in nominative. Context determines the gender.

prompt_data.rule: All plural nouns use 'die' regardless of gender

knowledge_points.explanation: In the plural, all genders use 'die': der Mann → die Männer, die Frau → die Frauen, das Kind → die Kinder.

prompt_data.rule: There is no plural indefinite article; use 'keine' to negate

knowledge_points.explanation: German has no plural indefinite article. Use 'keine' for negation: 'keine Bücher' = no books.
'der Hund' is masculine. Many animal names must be memorized for gender.

topics.name: Present Tense Regular Verbs
topics.description: Conjugating regular verbs in present tense: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en

knowledge_points.explanation: For 'ich', remove '-en' and add '-e': spielen → spiele.
For 'du', remove '-en' and add '-st': spielen → spielst.
For 'er/sie/es', remove '-en' and add '-t': lernen → lernt.
For 'wir', the verb stays the same as the infinitive: wohnen → wohnen.
For 'ihr', remove '-en' and add '-t': machen → macht.
For 'sie/Sie', the verb stays the same as the infinitive: kaufen → kaufen.
For 'ich': trinken → trinke. Regular pattern: remove '-en', add '-e'.
For 'du': lernen → lernst. Regular pattern: remove '-en', add '-st'.
When the stem ends in '-t' or '-d', add an extra '-e-' before the ending: arbeiten → arbeitet (not 'arbeitt').
When the stem ends in '-t', add '-est' for 'du': arbeiten → arbeitest.
For 'sie' (she): wohnen → wohnt. Same '-t' ending as 'er' and 'es'.
For 'ich': machen → mache. 'machen' is one of the most common German verbs.

topics.name: Negation
topics.description: Using 'nicht' and 'kein/keine/keinen' to form negative sentences

prompt_data.rule: Use 'nicht' to negate verbs — place it after the conjugated verb

knowledge_points.explanation: 'nicht' negates verbs. It usually comes at the end of a simple sentence or before what it specifically negates.

prompt_data.rule: Use 'nicht' before adjectives and adverbs to negate them

knowledge_points.explanation: 'nicht' comes directly before the adjective it negates: 'nicht groß', 'nicht schön'.

prompt_data.rule: Use 'kein' instead of 'nicht ein' for masculine and neuter nouns in nominative

knowledge_points.explanation: 'kein' replaces 'nicht ein'. For masculine/neuter nominative: 'ein' → 'kein'.

prompt_data.rule: Use 'keine' instead of 'nicht eine' for feminine nouns

knowledge_points.explanation: 'keine' replaces 'nicht eine' for feminine nouns: 'eine Katze' → 'keine Katze'.

prompt_data.rule: Use 'keine' to negate plural nouns

knowledge_points.explanation: 'keine' is used for all plural negations regardless of the original gender.

prompt_data.rule: Use 'keinen' for masculine nouns in the accusative case

knowledge_points.explanation: 'keinen' is the accusative masculine form: 'einen Hund' → 'keinen Hund'.

prompt_data.rule: 'nicht' goes at the end of the clause, or before the specific element being negated

knowledge_points.explanation: Default position for 'nicht' is at the end of the clause. If negating something specific, 'nicht' goes directly before it.

prompt_data.rule: Use 'kein' for nouns with ein/eine or no article; use 'nicht' for everything else
prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich trinke keinen Kaffee. Ich trinke nicht gern.
prompt_data.counter_example: Ich trinke einen Kaffee. Ich trinke gern.

knowledge_points.explanation: Rule of thumb: if the positive sentence has 'ein/eine' or no article before a noun, use 'kein'. Otherwise use 'nicht'.

topics.name: Basic Question Formation
topics.description: W-questions (Was, Wer, Wo, Wie, Wann, Woher, Wohin) and yes/no question structure

prompt_data.rule: Use 'Was' to ask about things or actions

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Was' asks about things or actions. The verb comes directly after: 'Was + verb + subject?'

prompt_data.rule: Use 'Wer' to ask about people (nominative)

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Wer' asks about people in nominative case. The verb is conjugated for 3rd person singular.

prompt_data.rule: Use 'Wo' to ask about location (static position)

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Wo' asks about a static location (where something is). Not to be confused with 'Wohin' (where to).

prompt_data.rule: Use 'Wie' to ask about manner, condition, or name

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Wie' means 'how' but also appears in 'Wie heißt du?' (What is your name? — literally 'How are you called?').

prompt_data.rule: Use 'Wann' to ask about time

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Wann' asks about a point in time: 'Wann beginnt der Kurs?'

prompt_data.rule: Use 'Woher' to ask about origin

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Woher' asks about origin. The standard answer uses 'aus': 'Ich komme aus Deutschland.'

prompt_data.rule: Use 'Wohin' to ask about destination or direction

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Wohin' asks about direction or destination: 'Wohin fährst du?' — 'Nach Berlin.'

topics.name: Possessive Adjectives
topics.description: Possessive adjectives: mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr

prompt_data.rule: 'mein' takes the same endings as 'ein': mein (m/n), meine (f/pl)

knowledge_points.explanation: 'mein' = my. It follows 'ein'-endings: mein Hund (m), meine Katze (f), mein Kind (n), meine Kinder (pl).

prompt_data.rule: 'dein' follows the same pattern as 'mein'

knowledge_points.explanation: 'dein' = your (informal). Same endings as 'mein': dein Vater, deine Mutter, dein Haus.

prompt_data.rule: 'sein' is used for masculine and neuter possessors

knowledge_points.explanation: 'sein' = his/its. Refers to a masculine or neuter possessor: 'Der Mann und sein Hund.'

prompt_data.rule: 'ihr' (lowercase) means 'her' or 'their' depending on context

knowledge_points.explanation: 'ihr' (lowercase) = her/their. Same form for both: 'Die Frau und ihr Kind' / 'Die Eltern und ihr Kind.'

prompt_data.rule: 'unser' takes ein-endings: unser (m/n), unsere (f/pl)

knowledge_points.explanation: 'unser' = our. Follows ein-endings: unser Vater, unsere Mutter, unser Kind, unsere Kinder.

prompt_data.rule: 'euer' loses the second 'e' when an ending is added: eure (not euere)

knowledge_points.explanation: 'euer' = your (plural informal). Note: with endings, the middle 'e' drops: eure Mutter (not euere).

prompt_data.rule: 'Ihr' (capitalized) is the formal possessive for 'Sie'
prompt_data.example_sentence: Ist das Ihr Koffer, Herr Schmidt?

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Ihr' (capitalized) = your (formal). Always capitalized to distinguish from 'ihr' (her/their).

prompt_data.rule: Add '-e' to possessives for feminine and plural nouns in nominative

knowledge_points.explanation: For feminine and plural nouns in nominative, add '-e': mein → meine, dein → deine, sein → seine.

topics.name: Accusative Case
topics.description: Accusative articles (den, die, das, einen, eine, ein) for direct objects

prompt_data.rule: Masculine definite article changes from 'der' to 'den' in accusative

knowledge_points.explanation: Only masculine changes in accusative: der → den. Feminine, neuter, and plural stay the same.

prompt_data.rule: Feminine article stays 'die' in accusative — no change
prompt_data.counter_example: Die Zeitung liegt auf dem Tisch.

knowledge_points.explanation: Feminine articles don't change in accusative: die Zeitung (nom.) → die Zeitung (acc.).

prompt_data.rule: Neuter article stays 'das' in accusative — no change

knowledge_points.explanation: Neuter articles don't change in accusative: das Buch (nom.) → das Buch (acc.).

prompt_data.rule: Masculine indefinite article changes from 'ein' to 'einen' in accusative

knowledge_points.explanation: Masculine indefinite: ein → einen in accusative. 'Ich kaufe einen Apfel.'

prompt_data.rule: Feminine indefinite article stays 'eine' in accusative — no change
prompt_data.counter_example: Eine Tasse steht auf dem Tisch.

knowledge_points.explanation: Feminine indefinite doesn't change in accusative: eine Katze (nom.) → eine Katze (acc.).

prompt_data.rule: Neuter indefinite article stays 'ein' in accusative — no change

knowledge_points.explanation: Neuter indefinite doesn't change in accusative: ein Buch (nom.) → ein Buch (acc.).

prompt_data.rule: The accusative case marks the direct object — the thing being acted upon

knowledge_points.explanation: The direct object (what receives the action) takes accusative: 'Ich sehe den Hund' — 'den Hund' is what I see.
'er' becomes 'ihn' in accusative: 'Der Mann? Ich sehe ihn.'

prompt_data.rule: 'ich' becomes 'mich' and 'du' becomes 'dich' in accusative
prompt_data.example_sentence: Er sieht mich. Ich sehe dich.
prompt_data.counter_example: Ich bin hier. Du bist da.

knowledge_points.explanation: Accusative pronouns: ich → mich, du → dich, er → ihn, sie → sie, es → es, wir → uns, ihr → euch, sie/Sie → sie/Sie.

prompt_data.rule: 'es' stays 'es' in accusative — no change for neuter pronouns
prompt_data.example_sentence: Das Buch? Ich lese es gerade.

knowledge_points.explanation: Neuter pronoun 'es' doesn't change in accusative: 'Ich brauche es.'

prompt_data.rule: 'wir' becomes 'uns' and 'ihr' becomes 'euch' in accusative
prompt_data.example_sentence: Er besucht uns morgen. Ich besuche euch nächste Woche.
prompt_data.counter_example: Wir sind hier. Ihr seid dort.

knowledge_points.explanation: Plural accusative pronouns: wir → uns, ihr → euch.

prompt_data.rule: The verb 'haben' always takes an accusative object
prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze.
prompt_data.counter_example: Ein Hund und eine Katze sind im Garten.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'haben' always requires accusative: 'Ich habe einen Bruder' (not 'ein Bruder').

topics.name: Accusative Prepositions
topics.description: Prepositions that always take the accusative case: durch, für, gegen, ohne, um

prompt_data.rule: 'für' always takes the accusative case
prompt_data.example_sentence: Das Geschenk ist für meinen Vater.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'für' (for) always requires accusative: 'für den Mann', 'für die Frau', 'für das Kind'.

prompt_data.rule: 'ohne' always takes the accusative case

knowledge_points.explanation: 'ohne' (without) takes accusative: 'ohne einen Fehler', 'ohne mich'.

prompt_data.rule: 'durch' always takes the accusative case

knowledge_points.explanation: 'durch' (through) takes accusative: 'durch den Wald', 'durch die Stadt'.

prompt_data.rule: 'gegen' always takes the accusative case
prompt_data.example_sentence: Wir spielen gegen die andere Mannschaft.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'gegen' (against) takes accusative. Also used for approximate time: 'gegen acht Uhr' (around 8 o'clock).

prompt_data.rule: 'um' always takes the accusative case
prompt_data.example_sentence: Der Kurs beginnt um neun Uhr.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'um' (around/at) takes accusative. Very common for clock times: 'um acht Uhr' (at 8 o'clock).

prompt_data.rule: Remember accusative prepositions with the mnemonic DOGFU: Durch, Ohne, Gegen, Für, Um
prompt_data.example_sentence: Durch den Park, ohne dich, gegen den Wind, für mich, um die Ecke.
prompt_data.counter_example: mit, bei, nach, von, zu (dative prepositions)

knowledge_points.explanation: The mnemonic DOGFU helps remember all five accusative prepositions: Durch, Ohne, Gegen, Für, Um.

topics.name: Basic Adjectives in Nominative
topics.description: Common adjectives used predicatively and with nominative articles

knowledge_points.explanation: 'groß' means big or tall. Predicative adjectives (after 'sein') take no ending: 'Der Mann ist groß.'
'klein' is the opposite of 'groß'. No ending when used predicatively: 'Das Kind ist klein.'
'alt' means old. Used for both people and things: 'Wie alt bist du?' (How old are you?)
'neu' is the opposite of 'alt' for things. For people, use 'jung' (young).
'gut' means good. Very common: 'Guten Morgen!' (Good morning), 'Alles gut' (All good).
'schlecht' is the opposite of 'gut'. 'Mir geht es schlecht' = I'm not doing well.
'schön' means beautiful or nice. Also used as an exclamation: 'Schön!' (Nice!/Great!).
'teuer' means expensive. Opposite: 'billig' (cheap) or 'günstig' (affordable).
'billig' means cheap. Can have a slightly negative connotation; 'günstig' (affordable) is more neutral.

prompt_data.rule: Adjectives before nouns need endings; after 'sein' they don't
prompt_data.example_sentence: Ein großer Mann steht dort. Der Mann ist groß.

knowledge_points.explanation: Predicative (after sein): no ending ('Der Tisch ist groß'). Attributive (before noun): ending required ('ein großer Tisch').

topics.name: Plural Forms
topics.description: Common German plural patterns: -e, -en, -er, -s, umlaut changes

prompt_data.rule: Many masculine and some neuter nouns add '-e' in plural

knowledge_points.explanation: The '-e' plural is common for masculine nouns: der Freund → die Freunde, der Tag → die Tage.

prompt_data.rule: Most feminine nouns add '-(e)n' in plural
prompt_data.example_sentence: die Lampe → die Lampen, die Frau → die Frauen

knowledge_points.explanation: The '-(e)n' plural is the most common for feminine nouns: die Blume → die Blumen, die Schwester → die Schwestern.

prompt_data.rule: Some neuter and masculine nouns add '-er', often with an umlaut
prompt_data.example_sentence: das Kind → die Kinder, das Buch → die Bücher

knowledge_points.explanation: The '-er' plural often adds an umlaut: das Haus → die Häuser, der Mann → die Männer.

prompt_data.rule: Foreign words and some informal words add '-s' in plural
prompt_data.example_sentence: das Auto → die Autos, das Hotel → die Hotels

knowledge_points.explanation: The '-s' plural is used mainly for foreign/borrowed words: das Kino → die Kinos, das Sofa → die Sofas.

prompt_data.rule: Some nouns change their vowel (a→ä, o→ö, u→ü) in plural, sometimes with no other ending
prompt_data.example_sentence: der Vater → die Väter, die Mutter → die Mütter

knowledge_points.explanation: Some nouns only change the vowel: der Bruder → die Brüder, die Tochter → die Töchter.

prompt_data.rule: Some masculine/neuter nouns ending in '-er', '-el', '-en' don't change in plural
prompt_data.example_sentence: das Fenster → die Fenster, der Lehrer → die Lehrer

knowledge_points.explanation: Nouns ending in '-er', '-el', '-en' often stay the same: der Computer → die Computer, das Zimmer → die Zimmer.

prompt_data.rule: All plural nouns use the article 'die' regardless of their singular gender
prompt_data.example_sentence: der Hund → die Hunde, die Katze → die Katzen, das Kind → die Kinder
prompt_data.counter_example: der Hund, die Katze, das Kind (singular)

knowledge_points.explanation: In plural, the article is always 'die': der/die/das all become 'die' in the plural.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Die Tiere im Zoo sind schön.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'das Tier' → 'die Tiere'. Neuter noun with '-e' plural ending.
'der Apfel' → 'die Äpfel'. Masculine noun with umlaut-only plural.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Die Städte in Deutschland sind interessant.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'die Stadt' → 'die Städte'. Feminine noun with umlaut + '-e' plural.

topics.name: Irregular Present Tense (Stem-Changing Verbs)
topics.description: Stem-changing verbs in present tense: fahren, sehen, lesen, sprechen, essen, nehmen, schlafen

knowledge_points.explanation: 'fahren' has a→ä change for du/er: du fährst, er fährt. Other forms are regular.
For er/sie/es: fahren → fährt (a→ä stem change).
'sehen' has e→ie change for du/er: du siehst, er sieht.
For er/sie/es: sehen → sieht (e→ie stem change).
'lesen' has e→ie change for du/er: du liest, er liest. Note: 'du liest' and 'er liest' look the same.
'sprechen' has e→i change for du/er: du sprichst, er spricht.
For er/sie/es: sprechen → spricht (e→i stem change).
'essen' has e→i change and an extra 's': du isst (not 'esst'). Note: 'du isst' and 'er isst' look the same.
'nehmen' is highly irregular: du nimmst, er nimmt (e→i plus mm).
'schlafen' has a→ä change for du/er: du schläfst, er schläft.

topics.name: Modal Verbs
topics.description: Modal verbs können, möchten, wollen, müssen and their sentence structure

knowledge_points.explanation: 'können' (can/to be able to): ich kann, du kannst, er kann. The umlaut disappears in singular.
Plural forms keep the umlaut: wir können, ihr könnt, sie können.
'möchten' (would like) is polite for requests: ich möchte, du möchtest, er möchte.
'möchten' is the polite way to order in restaurants: 'Ich möchte bitte eine Suppe.'
'wollen' (to want): ich will, du willst, er will. More direct/forceful than 'möchten'.
'müssen' (must/have to): ich muss, du musst, er muss. Expresses necessity or obligation.
Plural forms keep the umlaut: wir müssen, ihr müsst, sie müssen.

prompt_data.rule: Modal verb is conjugated in position 2; the main verb goes to the end as infinitive

knowledge_points.explanation: With modal verbs, the main verb goes to the end as infinitive: 'Ich muss morgen früh aufstehen.'
For 'du': können → kannst. The umlaut ö disappears in singular forms.

prompt_data.rule: 'nicht müssen' means 'don't have to', NOT 'must not'. For 'must not' use 'nicht dürfen'
prompt_data.example_sentence: Du musst nicht kommen. (You don't have to come.)
prompt_data.counter_example: Du darfst nicht rauchen. (You must not smoke.)

knowledge_points.explanation: Warning: 'nicht müssen' = don't have to (no obligation). 'nicht dürfen' = must not (forbidden).

topics.name: Imperatives
topics.description: Imperative forms for du, ihr, and Sie with common verbs

prompt_data.rule: For 'du': use the verb stem (remove -en, drop the -st ending). No pronoun.

knowledge_points.explanation: du-imperative: take the stem of the verb. kommen → Komm! machen → Mach! spielen → Spiel!

prompt_data.rule: For 'ihr': use the normal 'ihr' conjugation without the pronoun

knowledge_points.explanation: ihr-imperative = the 'ihr' form without the pronoun: Kommt! Macht! Spielt!

prompt_data.rule: For 'Sie': use infinitive + Sie. The pronoun stays.

knowledge_points.explanation: Sie-imperative: infinitive + Sie. Always includes the pronoun: Kommen Sie! Machen Sie! Sprechen Sie!
du-imperative of 'gehen': Geh! ihr: Geht! Sie: Gehen Sie!
Stem-changing e→ie verbs keep the change in du-imperative: lesen → Lies! sehen → Sieh!
Stem-changing e→i verbs keep the change: sprechen → Sprich! essen → Iss! nehmen → Nimm!
'sein' is irregular in imperative: du → Sei! ihr → Seid! Sie → Seien Sie!
ihr-imperative of 'machen': Macht! Same as the normal 'ihr' form without the pronoun.

topics.name: Numbers and Time
topics.description: Numbers 0-100, telling time with Uhr, and common time expressions

prompt_data.german: null, eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn

knowledge_points.explanation: Numbers 0-10 must be memorized. Note: 'eins' when counting, but 'ein/eine' before nouns.
'elf' (11) and 'zwölf' (12) are irregular — they don't follow the '-zehn' pattern.

prompt_data.rule: Numbers 13-19: digit + zehn (like English '-teen')
prompt_data.correct_form: dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn, sechzehn, siebzehn, achtzehn, neunzehn

knowledge_points.explanation: 13-19 follow the pattern: digit + zehn. Note: sechzehn (not 'sechszehn'), siebzehn (not 'siebenzehn').
'zwanzig' (20). Tens from 20 use '-zig': zwanzig, dreißig, vierzig...

prompt_data.rule: For 21-99: ones FIRST + und + tens (reverse of English)
prompt_data.example_sentence: Meine Großmutter ist fünfundsiebzig Jahre alt.

knowledge_points.explanation: German reverses the order: 25 = fünfundzwanzig (five-and-twenty). This takes practice!

prompt_data.german: dreißig, vierzig, fünfzig, sechzig, siebzig, achtzig, neunzig, hundert

knowledge_points.explanation: Note: dreißig (30) uses '-ßig' not '-zig'. Sechzig (not sechszig), siebzig (not siebenzig).

prompt_data.rule: Tell time with: Es ist + number + Uhr

knowledge_points.explanation: Basic time: 'Es ist acht Uhr' (It's 8 o'clock). For minutes: 'Es ist acht Uhr dreißig' (8:30).

prompt_data.english: half past (but references the NEXT hour)
prompt_data.rule: 'halb' + next hour means 30 minutes before that hour

knowledge_points.explanation: Warning: 'halb drei' = 2:30 (NOT 3:30)! 'halb' refers to halfway to the next hour.

prompt_data.rule: Use 'Viertel nach' for :15 and 'Viertel vor' for :45

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Viertel nach zehn' = 10:15. 'Viertel vor elf' = 10:45.

prompt_data.rule: Use 'um' to express 'at' a specific time
prompt_data.example_sentence: Der Kurs beginnt um neun Uhr.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'um' indicates a specific time: 'Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.' (I get up at 7 o'clock).

prompt_data.english: in the morning, at noon, in the evening, at night

knowledge_points.explanation: Time-of-day adverbs end in '-s': morgens (in the morning), abends (in the evening), nachts (at night).
'heute' = today, 'morgen' = tomorrow, 'gestern' = yesterday. Don't confuse 'morgen' (tomorrow) with 'der Morgen' (the morning).

topics.name: Word Order in Statements
topics.description: Basic German sentence structure: SVO, verb-second rule, and time-manner-place order

prompt_data.rule: In German statements, the conjugated verb is ALWAYS in position 2

knowledge_points.explanation: The V2 (verb-second) rule is fundamental: the conjugated verb must be the second element in a statement.

prompt_data.rule: When a non-subject starts the sentence, the subject moves after the verb (verb stays in position 2)

knowledge_points.explanation: If time or another element comes first, the subject flips to after the verb: 'Heute lerne ich Deutsch.'

prompt_data.rule: In the middle field, elements follow the order: Time – Manner – Place
prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich fahre morgen schnell nach Berlin.
prompt_data.counter_example: Ich fahre nach Berlin morgen schnell. (unnatural)

knowledge_points.explanation: German uses T-M-P order: WHEN → HOW → WHERE. 'Ich gehe heute gern ins Kino.'

prompt_data.rule: In sentences without a specific element to negate, 'nicht' goes at the end

knowledge_points.explanation: Default position for 'nicht' is at the end: 'Er kommt heute nicht.' But before adjectives/prepositions: 'Er ist nicht müde.'

prompt_data.rule: Time expressions can start the sentence for emphasis; the verb must still be in position 2
prompt_data.example_sentence: Am Montag habe ich einen Termin.
prompt_data.counter_example: Ich habe am Montag einen Termin.

knowledge_points.explanation: Both 'Ich lerne morgen Deutsch' and 'Morgen lerne ich Deutsch' are correct. The emphasis shifts.

prompt_data.rule: When a modal verb or auxiliary is used, the infinitive goes to the end of the sentence

knowledge_points.explanation: With modals, the infinitive goes to the very end: 'Ich muss heute viel arbeiten.'

topics.name: Sentence Connectors
topics.description: Coordinating conjunctions: und, aber, oder, denn — connecting clauses without changing word order

prompt_data.rule: 'und' connects words, phrases, or clauses without changing word order
prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich lerne Deutsch und er lernt Spanisch.
prompt_data.counter_example: Ich lerne Deutsch. Er lernt Spanisch.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'und' (and) is a coordinating conjunction: it connects two equal parts without affecting word order.

prompt_data.rule: 'aber' expresses contrast without changing word order
prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich möchte kommen, aber ich habe keine Zeit.
prompt_data.counter_example: Ich möchte kommen. Ich habe keine Zeit.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'aber' (but) introduces a contrast: 'Das Essen ist gut, aber teuer.'

prompt_data.rule: 'oder' presents alternatives without changing word order
prompt_data.counter_example: Möchtest du Tee? Möchtest du Kaffee?

knowledge_points.explanation: 'oder' (or) presents choices: 'Kommst du am Montag oder am Dienstag?'

prompt_data.rule: 'denn' gives a reason without changing word order in the following clause
prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin krank.
prompt_data.counter_example: Ich bleibe zu Hause. Ich bin krank.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'denn' (because) is a coordinating conjunction — word order stays normal: '..., denn + Subject + Verb + ...'

prompt_data.rule: Use a comma before 'aber', 'denn', and 'oder'/'und' when connecting full clauses
prompt_data.example_sentence: Er ist nett, aber manchmal laut.

knowledge_points.explanation: A comma is typically placed before 'aber' and 'denn'. Before 'und' and 'oder', a comma is optional when connecting full clauses.

prompt_data.rule: und, aber, oder, denn do NOT change word order — the verb stays in position 2 in both clauses
prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich koche, und du räumst auf.
prompt_data.counter_example: Ich koche, weil du aufräumst. (subordinating — different!)

knowledge_points.explanation: Coordinating conjunctions (und, aber, oder, denn) connect equal clauses. The word order stays the same in both clauses.

topics.name: Greetings & Basics
topics.description: Essential greetings, farewells, and polite expressions

knowledge_points.explanation: Universal informal greeting, used any time of day.
Used in the morning until about noon.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Guten Tag, mein Name ist Schmidt.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Guten Tag' is a polite, formal greeting used during the day.
Used from late afternoon/evening onward.
Said when going to bed, not as a general evening greeting.
Informal farewell, used with friends and acquaintances.
Formal farewell. Literally: 'Until we see each other again.'
'Bitte' means both 'please' and 'you're welcome' depending on context.
'Danke' is informal. 'Danke schön' or 'Vielen Dank' are more polite.
'Entschuldigung' is used to get attention or to apologize. Also: 'Entschuldigen Sie bitte' (more formal).
'ja' = yes, 'nein' = no. Also: 'doch' = yes (contradicting a negative question).

prompt_data.example_sentence: Guten Tag! Wie geht es Ihnen?

knowledge_points.explanation: Formal: 'Wie geht es Ihnen?' Informal: 'Wie geht's?' or 'Wie geht es dir?'
Standard response to 'Wie geht es dir/Ihnen?' Also: 'Gut, danke!' (shorter).
'Bis bald' = see you soon. Also: 'Bis morgen' (see you tomorrow), 'Bis später' (see you later).
'Ich heiße...' (My name is...). Alternative: 'Mein Name ist...' (more formal).

topics.name: Numbers 0-100
topics.description: Cardinal numbers from 0 to 100

knowledge_points.explanation: 'null' = zero. Used in phone numbers, temperatures, and scores.
'eins' when counting; 'ein/eine' before nouns: 'ein Buch', 'eine Tasse'.
'zwei' = two. On the phone, sometimes 'zwo' is used to avoid confusion with 'drei'.
'drei' = three.
'zehn' = ten. Base for teens: dreizehn (13), vierzehn (14), etc.
'zwanzig' = twenty. First of the '-zig' tens.
'dreißig' = thirty. Note: uses '-ßig' (not '-zig'). The only ten with this exception.
'fünfzig' = fifty.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Mein Opa ist siebzig Jahre alt.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'siebzig' = seventy. Note: 'siebzig' (not 'siebenzig').
'hundert' = one hundred. Can also say 'einhundert' for emphasis.
Remember: ones come first in German! 35 = fünf-und-dreißig (five-and-thirty).

prompt_data.example_sentence: Meine Nummer ist null eins sieben sechs...

knowledge_points.explanation: Phone numbers are usually read digit by digit: 0176 = null eins sieben sechs.

topics.name: Family Members
topics.description: Core family vocabulary with articles and plurals

knowledge_points.explanation: 'die Mutter' is feminine. Plural: die Mütter (with umlaut). Informal: 'die Mama'.
'der Vater' is masculine. Plural: die Väter (with umlaut). Informal: 'der Papa'.
'die Schwester' is feminine. Plural: die Schwestern.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Mein Bruder ist zehn Jahre alt.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Bruder' is masculine. Plural: die Brüder (with umlaut).

prompt_data.example_sentence: Meine Großmutter wohnt auf dem Land.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'die Großmutter' is feminine. Informal: 'die Oma'.
'der Großvater' is masculine. Informal: 'der Opa'.
'die Tante' is feminine. Plural: die Tanten.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Mein Onkel hat ein großes Auto.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Onkel' is masculine. Plural stays the same: die Onkel.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Das Kind geht in die Schule.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'das Kind' is neuter. Plural: die Kinder.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Meine Eltern kommen aus der Türkei.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'die Eltern' is always plural (no singular form). It means 'parents'.

topics.name: Food & Drink
topics.description: Common food and beverage vocabulary

knowledge_points.explanation: 'das Brot' is neuter. Bread is a staple of German cuisine — Germany has over 300 types!

prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich möchte ein Brot mit Käse.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Käse' is masculine. Plural is the same: die Käse.
'die Milch' is feminine. Usually uncountable (no common plural).
'der Kaffee' is masculine. Germans are among the world's top coffee consumers.
'der Tee' is masculine. Very popular in northern Germany (Ostfriesland).

prompt_data.example_sentence: Kann ich ein Glas Wasser haben?

knowledge_points.explanation: 'das Wasser' is neuter. In restaurants, ask for 'Leitungswasser' for tap water.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Der Apfel ist rot und süß.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Apfel' is masculine. Plural with umlaut: die Äpfel.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Zum Frühstück esse ich ein Ei.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'das Ei' is neuter. Plural: die Eier.
'das Fleisch' is neuter. Usually uncountable (no common plural).
'der Reis' is masculine. Usually uncountable.
'die Suppe' is feminine. Plural: die Suppen.
'das Bier' is neuter. Germany has a rich beer culture with over 1,500 breweries.
'das Obst' is neuter. A collective noun (no common plural). Individual fruits have their own articles.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich kaufe frisches Gemüse auf dem Markt.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'das Gemüse' is neuter. A collective noun for vegetables.
'der Kuchen' is masculine. Plural stays the same: die Kuchen. 'Kaffee und Kuchen' is a German afternoon tradition.

topics.name: Daily Routines
topics.description: Verbs and expressions for daily activities

prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'aufstehen' is a separable verb: 'Ich stehe auf.' The prefix 'auf-' goes to the end.
'frühstücken' = to have breakfast. Related: 'das Frühstück' (the breakfast).

prompt_data.example_sentence: Er arbeitet von neun bis fünf.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'arbeiten' = to work. Stem ends in '-t', so extra '-e-' in some forms: du arbeitest, er arbeitet.
'kochen' = to cook. Also means 'to boil': 'Das Wasser kocht.'
'schlafen' = to sleep. Stem-changing: du schläfst, er schläft.
'duschen' = to shower. Also reflexive: 'sich duschen'.
'einkaufen' is separable: 'Ich kaufe im Supermarkt ein.' Prefix 'ein-' goes to the end.
'fernsehen' is separable: 'Ich sehe fern.' Also stem-changing: du siehst fern, er sieht fern.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Am Wochenende putze ich die Wohnung.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'putzen' = to clean. 'Zähne putzen' = to brush teeth.
'lesen' = to read. Stem-changing: du liest, er liest.

topics.name: Home & Furniture
topics.description: Rooms, furniture, and household vocabulary

knowledge_points.explanation: 'die Küche' is feminine. Plural: die Küchen.
'das Wohnzimmer' is neuter. Compound: Wohn- (living) + Zimmer (room).
'das Schlafzimmer' is neuter. Compound: Schlaf- (sleep) + Zimmer (room).
'das Badezimmer' is neuter. Short form: 'das Bad'.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Das Essen steht auf dem Tisch.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Tisch' is masculine. Plural: die Tische.
'der Stuhl' is masculine. Plural with umlaut: die Stühle.
'das Bett' is neuter. 'ins Bett gehen' = to go to bed.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Die Katze liegt auf dem Sofa.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'das Sofa' is neuter. Plural: die Sofas (foreign word, takes -s).
'das Fenster' is neuter. Plural stays the same: die Fenster.
'die Tür' is feminine. Plural: die Türen.
'die Wohnung' is feminine. Most Germans rent rather than own: 'eine Wohnung mieten'.
'der Schrank' is masculine. Plural: die Schränke. 'Kleiderschrank' = wardrobe.

topics.name: Travel & Transport
topics.description: Vehicles, places, and travel-related vocabulary

prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich fahre mit dem Auto zur Arbeit.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'das Auto' is neuter. Short for 'das Automobil'. Plural: die Autos.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Der Bus kommt in fünf Minuten.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Bus' is masculine. Plural: die Busse (double 's').

prompt_data.example_sentence: Der Zug nach München fährt um zehn Uhr.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Zug' is masculine. Plural: die Züge (with umlaut).
'das Flugzeug' is neuter. Compound: Flug (flight) + Zeug (thing). Literally 'flying thing'.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich fahre mit dem Fahrrad zur Uni.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'das Fahrrad' is neuter. Short form: 'das Rad'. Very popular transport in Germany.
'die Straße' is feminine. Used in addresses: 'Berliner Straße 5'.
'der Bahnhof' is masculine. Compound: Bahn (railway) + Hof (yard/station).

prompt_data.example_sentence: Der Flughafen ist weit von der Stadt.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Flughafen' is masculine. Compound: Flug (flight) + Hafen (port/harbor).

prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich kaufe eine Fahrkarte am Automaten.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'die Fahrkarte' is feminine. Also: 'das Ticket' (more modern).

prompt_data.example_sentence: Die Haltestelle ist um die Ecke.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'die Haltestelle' is feminine. From 'halten' (to stop) + 'Stelle' (place).

topics.name: Hobbies & Leisure
topics.description: Sports, hobbies, and leisure activity vocabulary

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Sport' is masculine. 'Sport machen' or 'Sport treiben' = to do sports/exercise.
'die Musik' is feminine. 'Musik hören' = to listen to music. 'Musik machen' = to make music.
'schwimmen' = to swim. 'schwimmen gehen' = to go swimming.
'tanzen' = to dance. Regular verb: ich tanze, du tanzt, er tanzt.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Fußball ist in Deutschland sehr beliebt.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Fußball' is masculine. The most popular sport in Germany. 'Fußball spielen' = to play football.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Wir gehen heute Abend ins Kino.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'das Kino' is neuter. 'ins Kino gehen' = to go to the cinema.
'reisen' = to travel. Regular verb. 'die Reise' = the trip/journey.
'fotografieren' = to take photos. Inseparable verb (the stress is on '-ieren').
'spazieren gehen' = to go for a walk. Very common German leisure activity.
'gern' or 'gerne' (both correct) after a verb means 'to like doing something': 'Ich lese gern' = I like reading.

topics.name: Colors & Descriptions
topics.description: Basic color words and descriptive adjectives

knowledge_points.explanation: 'rot' = red. No ending when predicative: 'Das Auto ist rot.'
'blau' = blue. Colloquially, 'blau sein' = to be drunk.
'grün' = green. 'Die Grünen' = the Green Party in Germany.
'gelb' = yellow.
'weiß' = white. Don't confuse with 'weiß' (knows): 'Ich weiß das' = I know that.
'schwarz' = black. 'Schwarzwald' = Black Forest.
'groß' = big/tall. Comparative: größer. Superlative: am größten.
'klein' = small/short. Opposite of 'groß'.
'schön' = beautiful/nice. Very versatile: 'schönes Wetter', 'ein schöner Tag', 'Schön!' (Great!).
'braun' = brown.

topics.name: Days, Months, Seasons
topics.description: Days of the week, months of the year, and seasons

knowledge_points.explanation: All days are masculine ('der'). 'am Montag' = on Monday.
'der Dienstag' = Tuesday. All days of the week are masculine.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Mittwoch ist die Mitte der Woche.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Mittwoch' literally means 'mid-week' (Mitte + Woche).

prompt_data.example_sentence: Am Donnerstag gehe ich zum Sport.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Donnerstag' comes from 'Donner' (thunder) — named after the god of thunder.
'Freitag' comes from the goddess Freya.
'Samstag' (Saturday). In northern Germany also called 'Sonnabend'.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Am Sonntag haben die Geschäfte zu.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Sonntag' = Sunday. Most shops in Germany are closed on Sundays.
All months are masculine ('der'). 'im Januar' = in January.
'der März' = March. Note the umlaut: März (not Marz).
'der Juni' = June. Careful: 'Juni' vs. 'Juli' sound similar — Germans sometimes say 'Juno' and 'Julei' to distinguish.
'der Dezember' = December. Christmas markets ('Weihnachtsmärkte') are a highlight.
'der Frühling' = spring. Also called 'das Frühjahr'. 'im Frühling' = in spring.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Im Sommer fahren wir ans Meer.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Sommer' = summer. 'die Sommerferien' = summer holidays.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Im Herbst werden die Blätter bunt.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Herbst' = autumn/fall. Related to English 'harvest'.
'der Winter' = winter. 'im Winter' = in winter.

topics.name: Shopping & Commerce
topics.description: Shopping vocabulary: buying, prices, and stores

knowledge_points.explanation: 'kaufen' = to buy. Regular verb: ich kaufe, du kaufst, er kauft.
'der Preis' is masculine. 'Wie viel kostet das?' = How much does that cost?
'der Euro' is masculine. In spoken German, the plural is often just 'Euro': 'fünf Euro'.
'der Cent' is masculine. 'drei Euro fünfzig' = 3.50 EUR.
'teuer' = expensive. Comparative: teurer. Opposite: 'billig' or 'günstig'.
'billig' = cheap. Can sound slightly negative; 'günstig' (affordable/good value) is more neutral.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Das Geschäft ist um die Ecke.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'das Geschäft' is neuter. Also means 'business' in general.
'der Supermarkt' is masculine. Common chains in Germany: Aldi, Lidl, Rewe, Edeka.
'bezahlen' = to pay. Also: 'zahlen' (shorter form). 'Kann ich mit Karte bezahlen?'
'kosten' = to cost. 'Wie viel kostet das?' and 'Was kostet das?' are both common.

topics.name: Professions
topics.description: Common job titles and professional vocabulary

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Arzt' (male), 'die Ärztin' (female). Most professions have feminine forms with '-in'.
'der Lehrer' (male), 'die Lehrerin' (female). Add '-in' for the feminine form.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Ich bin Student an der Universität.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'Student' is specifically for university students. For school pupils: 'der Schüler / die Schülerin'.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Der Koch bereitet das Essen vor.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Koch' (male), 'die Köchin' (female). Related to 'kochen' (to cook).

prompt_data.example_sentence: Sie arbeitet als Ingenieurin bei Siemens.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Ingenieur' (male), 'die Ingenieurin' (female). Germany is famous for its engineers.
'Verkäufer' from 'verkaufen' (to sell). '-er' for doer of the action, '-in' for feminine.

prompt_data.example_sentence: Der Polizist steht an der Kreuzung.

knowledge_points.explanation: 'der Polizist' (male), 'die Polizistin' (female). Note: 'die Polizei' = the police (institution).
Traditional: 'Krankenschwester' (f). Modern gender-neutral: 'Pflegefachkraft'. Male: 'Krankenpfleger'.
'der Beruf' = profession. 'Was sind Sie von Beruf?' = What do you do for a living?
'als' + profession (no article): 'Ich arbeite als Lehrerin.' NOT 'als eine Lehrerin'.
